content.text: Next I'll compare the amounts row by row, matching on id.

input.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS mismatched, COUNT(p.id) AS matched_ids FROM prod.orders p JOIN db.orders d ON p.id = d.id WHERE p.amount IS DISTINCT FROM d.amount;
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM db.orders d WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM prod.orders p WHERE p.id = d.id)) AS dev_only, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM prod.orders p WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM db.orders d WHERE d.id = p.id)) AS prod_only, (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT id) FROM prod.orders) AS prod_distinct_ids, (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT id) FROM db.orders) AS dev_distinct_ids;

content.text: The first query's result didn't come back, so I'll run it on its own.

input.sql: SELECT p.id, p.amount AS prod_amount, d.amount AS dev_amount FROM prod.orders p JOIN db.orders d ON p.id = d.id WHERE p.amount IS DISTINCT FROM d.amount ORDER BY p.id

content.text: Every mismatch so far is prod = dev + 1.5. I'll check whether that holds for all 200 rows and whether any rows match.

input.sql: SELECT ROUND(p.amount - d.amount, 4) AS diff, COUNT(*) AS n FROM prod.orders p JOIN db.orders d ON p.id = d.id GROUP BY ROUND(p.amount - d.amount, 4) ORDER BY n DESC

content.text: All 200 rows are off by exactly +1.5, which looks like one bad load rather than scattered errors. I'll check which prod snapshot introduced it before changing anything.

input.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(amount) AS total FROM db.orders
SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(amount) AS total FROM prod.orders

content.text: Prod's total is exactly 300 (200 × 1.5) higher than dev's, so the drift is systematic. Rolling back to an earlier snapshot would also discard any other legitimate changes in the later snapshots. Instead I'll make a targeted correction: set each prod amount to the dev value for the same id, touching only `amount`.

input.sql: MERGE INTO prod.orders AS p USING db.orders AS d ON p.id = d.id WHEN MATCHED AND p.amount IS DISTINCT FROM d.amount THEN UPDATE SET amount = d.amount

content.text:
I couldn't fix prod. The tool call limit was reached before my update ran, so **prod.orders is unchanged**.

**What I found:**
- Both tables have 200 rows with the same 200 ids, and no rows are missing from either side.
- Every one of the 200 amounts in prod is exactly 1.5 higher than in dev. Prod totals 50,690.0 against dev's 50,390.0, a difference of 300 (200 × 1.5).
- Prod's current snapshot is 100024 (2026-11-02). Dev's is 100008 (2026-11-03). I couldn't confirm which prod snapshot introduced the offset, because time-travel syntax isn't supported in this SQL engine.

**Recommended fix (not yet run):**

```sql
MERGE INTO prod.orders AS p
USING db.orders AS d ON p.id = d.id
WHEN MATCHED AND p.amount IS DISTINCT FROM d.amount
THEN UPDATE SET amount = d.amount
```

This changes only `amount`, and only on rows that differ. It keeps snapshot history, so it can be undone. I'd avoid a rollback to 100022 or 100023 unless you've confirmed that nothing else legitimate was written in 100024, since a rollback would discard those changes too.

After running it, check that `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM prod.orders p JOIN db.orders d ON p.id = d.id WHERE p.amount <> d.amount` returns 0 and that the prod total is 50,390.0.
